newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda refugees in Tanzania may go home too.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda refugees in Tanzania may go home too.

text.p: The United Nations is hopeful Rwandans in refugee camps in Tanzania will follow the example of refugees in Zaire and go home, but some say they are afraid of being arrested or killed if they return.

"I'm willing to go back, but I'm afraid that those who are repatriated are killed. I don't get any replies to letters I send (to friends and relatives)," said one refugee called Jean, who asked that his full name not be used.

The Rwandan Hutus refugees -- some 500,000 in the five sprawling Ngara camps -- fled their country in 1994 after Tusti-led rebels took over Rwanda in the wake of the mass killings of Tutsis by Hutu militia and mobs.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR says that many refugees were duped into not returning by Hutu extremists who claimed the new Tutsi-led government in Rwanda would be overthrown.
The return of about 600,000 refugees from Zaire the past month -- after Rwandan-backed rebels took control of eastern Zaire -- has weakened the influence of the extremists, UNHCR officials say.

About 10,000 of the refugees have returned home since the camps in northerwest Tanzania were set up but since the start of November the return of some 550, including former government officials, has raised hopes the others might also go back.

The decision two weeks ago by a former Rwandan district commissioner for Rusomo, Joseph Habimana, to return home -- given prominence on Rwandan radio -- prompted widespread discussion in the Benaco camps. He was the most senior refugee to return home so far.
"I believe within one year not half will still be here. The majority of Rwandans in my opinion will have gone back," said Musa Abiriga, the UNHCR head in Ngara.
Abiriga told Reuters this week that a key factor for refugees would be how those who left Zaire were resettled.
The Tanzanian government is also planning to relocate up to 200 Hutu extremists and intimidators to another camp as a further confidence-booster.

"My feeling is sometime after Christmas, certainly in the new year, we'll wake up in the morning and people will be packing their bags and walking," said Mark Richardson, spokesman for Care International, which assists with camp management.

But Tanzanian officials have kept open the possibility that the Rwandan refugees might be forced to go home. Kigoma Regional Commissioner Yusuf Makamba said in November that forced repatriation was an option.
"We (aid agencies) won't have any say -- it will be the refugee leaders or the Tanzanian government," Richardson said.

Last Thursday, 87 Rwandans decided to return home. They were a disparate group including peasants, aspiring businesswomen, unaccompanied minors and one woman who decided on the spur of the moment to leave her husband.
"We're not getting much assistance. It's better we go home," said a 19-year-old youth called Kulihingoma, barefoot and wearing tattered, torn-off jeans and a filthy cotton T-shirt,
Kulihingoma and his 15-year-old sister Wamahoro were waiting for their repatriation papers to be processed before boarding a bus that would take them on the short journey home from Benaco camp.
Their parents are both dead but they knew of an aunt who lived in Ruhengeri.

Julius Gahamanyi, 25, says he now wants to return home. "If the 500,000 (Rwandans from Zaire) are well-treated, given their property. If justice is returned and no one is ill-treated or repressed, people might repatriate in large numbers.
"I'm still optimistic, one day in Rwanda we'll live in peace. I did not plan to live as a refugee in Tanzania for three years," he said.
